---
title: "Technical Appendix: Summary Statistics"
---

This appendix develops the summary-statistics representation used by `sblr`
from the individual-level Gaussian regression model. It explains why a small
set of cross-products contains the likelihood information needed for BLR-style
marker updates, how BED-derived sufficient statistics are combined with sparse
LD in the CSR samplers, and which assumptions are required for single- and
multi-trait analyses.

The central principle is that the Gaussian likelihood depends on the observed
data through cross-products such as $X^\top y$, $X^\top X$, and $y^\top y$.
Replacing repeated access to individual-level data with these quantities can
preserve the marker-update algebra, but only when marker order, sample
definition, genotype coding, allele frequencies, and LD are mutually
compatible.

Throughout the Methods documentation, mathematical cross-products are written
explicitly. Code names such as `wy`, `Xy`, `ww`, `yy`, and `SSY` are used only
when referring to actual `sblr` inputs or outputs. This avoids giving historical
implementation names a separate mathematical meaning.

## Individual-Level Model and Cross-Product Sufficiency

For one centered phenotype, let

$$
y\in\mathbb{R}^{N},
\qquad
X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M},
\qquad
b\in\mathbb{R}^{M},
$$

and consider the model

$$
y=Xb+e,
\qquad
e\sim N(0,v_eI_N).
$$

Here $N$ is the number of individuals and $M$ is the number of markers.
Conditional on $b$ and $v_e$, the Gaussian log likelihood is, up to an additive
constant,

$$
\log p(y\mid b,v_e)
=
-\frac{1}{2v_e}(y-Xb)^\top(y-Xb).
$$

Expanding the residual sum of squares gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
(y-Xb)^\top(y-Xb)
&=
y^\top y
-2b^\top X^\top y
+b^\top X^\top Xb.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Gaussian regression likelihood can be evaluated from

$$
y^\top y,
\qquad
X^\top y,
\qquad
X^\top X,
\qquad
N,
$$

without repeatedly accessing every individual observation.

The prior may require additional quantities, but the marker-likelihood
calculations depend on the data only through these cross-products. This is the
sense in which they are sufficient for the Gaussian regression layer.

## Mathematical Quantities and Current Code Names

The mathematical notation and implementation names should be kept distinct.

| Mathematical quantity | Meaning | Current code names encountered in `sblr` |
|---|---|---|
| $X^\top y$ | marker-phenotype cross-product vector | commonly `wy` |
| $X^\top Y$ | marker-by-trait cross-product matrix | represented as trait-wise `wy` in some routes and `Xy` in some MT/native interfaces |
| $\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)$ | marker diagonal cross-products | `ww` |
| $y^\top y$ | phenotype sum of squares | `yy` |
| pairwise cross-trait phenotype products | trait cross-product information | commonly described as `SSY`; some interfaces carry the matrix through a `yy`/`YY` argument |

These names are implementation conventions. In the derivations below,
$X^\top y$, $X^\top Y$, and $X^\top X$ denote the statistical quantities
themselves.

For marker $j$, define the diagonal genotype cross-product

$$
w_j=x_j^\top x_j,
$$

where $x_j$ is column $j$ of $X$. In code, the vector
$(w_1,\ldots,w_M)^\top$ is stored as `ww`.

## Residual Scores and Marker Updates

Define the marker-scale residual score vector

$$
r
=
X^\top(y-Xb)
=
X^\top y-X^\top Xb.
$$

This is not the individual-level residual vector $y-Xb$. It is the projection
of that residual vector onto all marker columns.

For marker $j$, adding its current effect back to the residual score gives

$$
s_j=r_j+w_jb_j.
$$

Because

$$
r_j
=
x_j^\top y
-x_j^\top x_jb_j
-\sum_{\ell\ne j}x_j^\top x_\ell b_\ell,
$$

we obtain

$$
s_j
=
x_j^\top y
-\sum_{\ell\ne j}x_j^\top x_\ell b_\ell.
$$

Thus $s_j$ is the cross-product of marker $j$ with the phenotype residual
excluding marker $j$'s own current effect. BayesC-style activity and effect
updates depend on this score, $w_j$, the residual variance, and the relevant
prior parameters.

If marker $j$ changes from $b_j^{\mathrm{old}}$ to
$b_j^{\mathrm{new}}$, define

$$
\Delta b_j
=
b_j^{\mathrm{new}}-b_j^{\mathrm{old}}.
$$

Under the complete cross-product representation,

$$
r^{\mathrm{new}}
=
r^{\mathrm{old}}
-
(X^\top X)_{\cdot j}\Delta b_j.
$$

The diagonal entry updates as

$$
r_j^{\mathrm{new}}
=
r_j^{\mathrm{old}}
-
w_j\Delta b_j,
$$

and the remaining entries are adjusted according to the cross-products between
marker $j$ and the other markers.

In the CSR implementation, only retained LD neighbors receive the
off-diagonal part of this update. This is one of the places where sparse-LD
approximation changes the numerical likelihood state relative to a complete
$X^\top X$ representation.

## The Identity $X^\top Xb=X^\top y-r$

Rearranging the residual-score definition gives

$$
X^\top Xb
=
X^\top y-r.
$$

This identity is useful well beyond the marker update. It allows residual
variance, genomic variance, and marker- or set-level genetic contributions to
be calculated from summary-statistic quantities and the maintained residual
score.

### Residual sum of squares

Starting from

$$
\operatorname{SSE}
=
y^\top y
-2b^\top X^\top y
+b^\top X^\top Xb
$$

and substituting

$$
X^\top Xb=X^\top y-r
$$

gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SSE}
&=
y^\top y
-2b^\top X^\top y
+b^\top(X^\top y-r)\\
&=
y^\top y
-b^\top(X^\top y+r).
\end{aligned}
$$

The current single-trait CSR implementation uses the corresponding code
quantities `yy`, `wy`, `b`, and `r` to evaluate this expression without
returning to individual-level observations.

### Genomic variance

For centered genotypes, the fitted genetic values are

$$
g=Xb.
$$

Their quadratic form is

$$
g^\top g
=
b^\top X^\top Xb
=
b^\top(X^\top y-r).
$$

A natural sample-scaled genomic-variance quantity is therefore

$$
\widehat v_g
=
\frac{1}{N}
b^\top(X^\top y-r).
$$

The denominator $N$ makes this a cross-product-per-observation quantity; it is
not presented here as an unbiased sample-variance estimator. In the CSR code,
the same calculation is expressed using the stored `wy` vector and residual
score.

## Genotype Scaling, Allele Frequencies, and `ww`

Summary statistics and LD are meaningful only relative to the genotype matrix
that produced them.

Let $g_{ij}\in\{0,1,2\}$ be the dosage for individual $i$ at marker $j$, and
let $p_j$ be the supplied or estimated allele frequency. With
`bed_xtx_xty(..., scale = TRUE)`, the implemented marker coding is

$$
x_{ij}
=
\frac{g_{ij}-2p_j}
{\sqrt{2p_j(1-p_j)}}.
$$

Missing BED genotypes are mapped to zero on this standardized scale. Under the
supplied allele frequency this corresponds to mean imputation before
standardization.

For a nondegenerate marker and compatible sample,

$$
w_j=x_j^\top x_j
$$

is often close to the number of used individuals because the standardized
marker variance is approximately one. It is not assumed to equal $N$ exactly.
Realized allele counts, missingness, externally supplied allele frequencies,
and sample selection all affect $w_j$.

With `scale = FALSE`, the implementation uses raw dosage coding and mean
imputes missing values to $2p_j$. This path is intentionally uncentered.
Consequently, its cross-products and regression interpretation differ from
those of the standardized path unless centering is handled elsewhere.

Allele frequencies therefore define more than metadata: they participate in
the definition of the genotype matrix used to construct $X^\top y$,
$\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)$, and LD. Inconsistent allele frequencies
between sufficient-statistic and sparse-LD construction imply inconsistent
genotype representations.

## Dense Cross-Products, Correlation LD, and Sparse Reconstruction

The complete genotype cross-product matrix has entries

$$
(X^\top X)_{j\ell}
=
x_j^\top x_\ell.
$$

Its diagonal is supplied to the CSR samplers through `ww`. The disk-backed CSR
files produced by the sparse-LD workflow store retained correlations rather
than complete cross-products.

To avoid confusing an LD correlation with the residual-score vector $r$, write
the retained correlation between markers $j$ and $\ell$ as
$\rho_{j\ell}$. From this correlation and the diagonal cross-products, the
sampler reconstructs the retained off-diagonal cross-product as

$$
\widetilde C_{X,j\ell}
=
\rho_{j\ell}\sqrt{w_jw_\ell},
$$

where $\widetilde C_X$ denotes the sparse approximation to $X^\top X$ used by
the CSR likelihood. The diagonal is handled separately from `ww`.

With all correlations retained, compatible scaling, and compatible diagonal
cross-products,

$$
\widetilde C_X
=
X^\top X
$$

up to numerical precision. In practical sparse-LD analyses, thresholds and
windows remove entries, so instead

$$
\widetilde C_X
\approx
X^\top X.
$$

The residual score maintained by the sparse sampler is consequently

$$
r_{\mathrm{CSR}}
=
X^\top y-\widetilde C_Xb.
$$

When a weak or distant LD edge is omitted, an effect change at one marker does
not propagate through that omitted edge in the maintained residual score.
This is a statistical approximation, not merely a storage optimization.

See [Sparse LD and CSR](sparse_ld_csr.qmd) for the storage, thresholding, and
disk contracts.

## Computing Sufficient Statistics With `bed_xtx_xty()`

`bed_xtx_xty()` computes the sufficient statistics directly from selected
markers in one PLINK BED file. A short call is:

```r
stats <- bed_xtx_xty(
  bed_file = Glist$bedfiles[chr],
  n = Glist$n,
  cls = cls,
  af = Glist$af[[chr]][cls],
  y = y,
  rows = NULL,
  scale = TRUE
)
```

The main inputs have the following contracts:

- `bed_file` identifies the PLINK BED file.
- `n` is the number of individuals represented by that BED file.
- `cls` contains positive one-based BED marker indices in the desired model
  order.
- `af` contains allele frequencies in exactly the `cls` order. If omitted,
  frequencies are estimated from the selected individuals.
- `y` is an $N_{\mathrm{used}}\times T$ phenotype matrix for the individuals
  included in the calculation.
- `rows` optionally selects unique one-based BED rows; when supplied, `y` must
  contain exactly those selected individuals in the same order.
- `scale` selects standardized or raw-dosage marker coding.

For trait $t$, the mathematical quantities returned are

$$
X^\top y_t,
\qquad
\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X),
\qquad
y_t^\top y_t.
$$

The corresponding current code fields are `wy`, `ww`, and `yy`.

The same `ww` vector is repeated across traits because the current function
uses one selected genotype matrix $X$ for all phenotype columns. Additional
returned fields include `xx`, the allele frequencies used, row-selection
information, sample and marker counts, scaling status, and summaries of the
marker diagonal cross-products.

The output marker order is the input `cls` order. The function does not infer
the intended biological marker order from IDs, so the analysis order must be
established before the call.

## Combining `bed_xtx_xty()` With Sparse LD

The sufficient-statistic and LD branches must describe the same underlying
genotype matrix:

```text
same BED marker selection and order
+ same selected individuals
+ same allele frequencies and scaling
    -> compatible X'y, diag(X'X), y'y, and sparse LD
```

Here the text block uses compact transpose notation for readability; the
mathematical objects are $X^\top y$, $\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)$, and
$y^\top y$.

`make_sparse_ld()` constructs retained marker correlations from BED data,
writes them under a sparse-LD prefix, and records metadata in
`Glist$sparseLD`. It must use the same marker ordering, sample rows, allele
frequencies, and scaling convention used for the sufficient statistics. The
lower-level writer behind this workflow is `sparseLD_stream_CSR()`.

The current workflow handoff is represented by code-field names:

```text
BED + phenotype
  -> make_summary_stats() -> wy, ww, yy, n
  -> make_sparse_ld()     -> Glist$sparseLD
  -> stblr_csr(stats = stats, Glist = Glist)
```

The complete operational sequence is documented in
[Sparse-LD and individual-level workflows](../notes/sparse_ld_workflows.qmd).

## How `stblr_csr()` Consumes the Statistics

At the public interface, `stblr_csr()` accepts implementation objects such as:

- `stats$wy`, representing $X^\top y$ for each trait;
- `stats$ww`, representing $\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)$;
- `stats$yy`, representing $y^\top y$ for each trait;
- `n`, representing the associated sample size;
- `Glist$sparseLD$prefix`, or an explicit `ld_prefix`, identifying the
  compatible disk-backed sparse LD; and
- prior, variance-update, scheduling, and MCMC controls.

The wrapper uses `yy/(n-1)` to initialize phenotype-variance-related prior
scales. The native sampler validates marker and trait dimensions, reconstructs
retained off-diagonal cross-products from LD correlations and `ww`, and
initializes or rebuilds the sparse residual score

$$
r_{\mathrm{CSR}}
=
X^\top y-\widetilde C_Xb.
$$

Marker and variance updates are then performed from this
summary-statistic state.

For the current shared-LD parallel single-trait CSR path, `ww` and `n` must
agree across traits. This reflects one common genotype sample and scaling
scheme. Trait-specific summary statistics from materially different samples
require a likelihood and LD contract that explicitly supports those
differences.

## Multi-Trait Summary-Statistic Representation

For $T$ traits on one common set of $N$ individuals, collect phenotypes and
marker effects as

$$
Y=
\begin{bmatrix}
y_1 & \cdots & y_T
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times T},
$$

and

$$
B=
\begin{bmatrix}
b_1 & \cdots & b_T
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times T}.
$$

The individual-level model is

$$
Y=XB+E_Y,
$$

where $E_Y$ is the observation-level residual matrix. If individuals are
jointly observed for all traits, the rows of $E_Y$ may have residual covariance
matrix $V_e$.

The principal marker-by-trait cross-product is

$$
X^\top Y.
$$

Under complete sample overlap, the phenotype cross-product matrix is

$$
Y^\top Y.
$$

In code, the marker-trait quantity may be represented as trait-wise `wy` or
through a field such as `Xy`, depending on the interface. Cross-trait phenotype
products are commonly described as `SSY`; the next section defines the
mathematical object more carefully so that partial overlap can also be handled.

For a common $X$, define the marker-score matrix

$$
R
=
X^\top(Y-XB)
=
X^\top Y-X^\top XB.
$$

Column $t$ is the residual-score vector for trait $t$:

$$
r_t
=
X^\top y_t-X^\top Xb_t.
$$

Hence,

$$
X^\top Xb_t
=
X^\top y_t-r_t.
$$

A symmetric sample-scaled genomic covariance estimate for traits $t$ and $s$
can then be written as

$$
[\widehat V_g]_{ts}
=
\frac{1}{2\sqrt{N_tN_s}}
\left[
b_t^\top(X^\top y_s-r_s)
+
b_s^\top(X^\top y_t-r_t)
\right].
$$

When $t=s$, this reduces to the single-trait genomic-variance expression. When
all traits use the same sample size $N$, the denominator becomes $N$.

## Cross-Trait Phenotype Products and Sample Overlap

Separate marginal quantities $y_t^\top y_t$ do not determine
cross-trait phenotype products. This matters because a full residual covariance
update requires information about how phenotypes co-vary among individuals who
are observed for each trait pair.

For traits $t$ and $s$, let $\mathcal I_{ts}$ denote the set of individuals
observed for both traits, and let

$$
N_{ts}
=
|\mathcal I_{ts}|.
$$

Define the pairwise phenotype cross-product matrix $S_Y$ by

$$
[S_Y]_{ts}
=
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{ts}}
y_{it}y_{is}.
$$

Its diagonal is

$$
[S_Y]_{tt}
=
y_t^\top y_t.
$$

If all traits are measured on exactly the same individuals, then

$$
S_Y
=
Y^\top Y.
$$

Under partial overlap, however, different entries of $S_Y$ can be calculated
from different sets of individuals. In that case, $S_Y$ should not literally be
interpreted as the cross-product of one complete rectangular phenotype matrix.

The current code and documentation commonly refer to this trait
cross-product information as `SSY`. Here $S_Y$ is the mathematical object and
`SSY` is the implementation/documentation name.

For a common complete sample,

$$
(Y-XB)^\top(Y-XB)
=
Y^\top Y
-Y^\top XB
-B^\top X^\top Y
+B^\top X^\top XB.
$$

For pairwise-overlap summary information, the same role is played by $S_Y$
under the assumptions of the corresponding overlap reconstruction.

If phenotype covariance is homogeneous among contributing individuals, then

$$
\mathbb E\left([S_Y]_{ts}\right)
=
N_{ts}\sigma_{ts},
$$

where $\sigma_{ts}$ is the cross-trait phenotype covariance for traits $t$ and
$s$.

Given a phenotype correlation matrix $R_y$ and approximate marginal trait
variances

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(y_t)
\approx
\frac{y_t^\top y_t}{N_t},
$$

one may construct

$$
\widehat\sigma_{ts}
=
[R_y]_{ts}
\sqrt{
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(y_t)
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(y_s)
}
$$

and approximate

$$
\widehat S_Y
=
N_{\mathrm{overlap}}
\odot
\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(Y),
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{overlap}}=[N_{ts}]$ and $\odot$ denotes elementwise
multiplication. The diagonal should be forced to the observed marginal
cross-products $y_t^\top y_t$.

Full-overlap and fractional-overlap assumptions define different
$N_{\mathrm{overlap}}$ matrices and therefore different reconstructed
likelihood information. Incorrect cross-trait products or overlap assumptions
can distort residual covariance inference even when all marginal trait
statistics are individually valid.

The complete derivation and sensitivity considerations are given in
[Multi-Trait Sample Overlap](multitrait_overlap.qmd).

## Residual and Genomic Covariance From Multi-Trait Summary Scores

For a joint multi-trait model with one common $X$, the residual cross-product
matrix can be written as

$$
S_e
=
S_Y
-B^\top X^\top Y
-Y^\top XB
+B^\top X^\top XB.
$$

Using

$$
X^\top XB
=
X^\top Y-R,
$$

gives

$$
S_e
=
S_Y
-B^\top X^\top Y
-Y^\top XB
+B^\top(X^\top Y-R).
$$

Under a complete common sample, $S_Y=Y^\top Y$ and the expression is the
ordinary residual cross-product $(Y-XB)^\top(Y-XB)$. Under pairwise overlap,
the use of a reconstructed $S_Y$ is an approximation whose interpretation
depends on the overlap model and the assumptions described above.

Finite precision, asymmetric input construction, or trait-specific summary
statistics can make nominally equivalent cross-trait expressions differ
slightly by orientation. The current native multi-trait CSR implementation
symmetrizes off-diagonal residual and genomic covariance quantities before
covariance updates.

A vector of marginal `yy` values can support separate trait-wise residual
variance updates. It cannot, by itself, identify a full residual covariance
matrix.

## Set-Specific and LD-Aware Genetic Contributions

The identity

$$
X^\top Xb_t
=
X^\top y_t-r_t
$$

also supports descriptive marker- and set-level summaries.

For a marker set $\mathcal S_k$, define the fitted set-specific genomic
contribution for trait $t$ as

$$
\widehat v_{g,k,t}
=
\frac{1}{N_t}
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\widehat b_{jt}
\left[
X^\top y_t-r_t
\right]_j.
$$

The corresponding marker-level contribution is

$$
c_{jt}
=
\frac{
\widehat b_{jt}
\left[
X^\top y_t-r_t
\right]_j
}{N_t}.
$$

An optional PIP-weighted descriptive version is

$$
c^{\mathrm{weighted}}_{jt}
=
\frac{
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
\widehat b_{jt}
\left[
X^\top y_t-r_t
\right]_j
}{N_t}.
$$

In current fit objects, the posterior mean effects and PIPs are commonly
represented by `bm` and `dm`.

These quantities are useful for describing annotations, loci, or genomic
regions. For disjoint sets, the unweighted contributions can approximate a
partition of the fitted genomic-variance expression. For overlapping sets, one
marker contributes to every set containing it, so the resulting totals are
attributions rather than an additive partition.

There is also an important posterior-summarization caveat. Combining posterior
mean effects, posterior mean PIPs, and a returned residual score in a nonlinear
formula is generally not the same as calculating that quantity at every MCMC
draw and then averaging. Such summaries should therefore not be described as
exact posterior expectations unless they are calculated draw by draw.

See [Empirical-Bayes Construction](annotation_informed_models.qmd) for
annotation-level uses of these quantities.

## Exact Equivalence and Practical Differences

Suppose all of the following are exact and compatible:

- the same centered or otherwise identically coded genotype matrix $X$;
- the same phenotype $y$;
- complete $X^\top y$, $y^\top y$, and $X^\top X$;
- the same prior, initialization, and variance model; and
- the same update schedule and numerical parameterization.

Then individual-level and summary-statistic marker updates can target the same
Gaussian regression model because the likelihood calculations are
algebraically equivalent.

Practical BED and CSR fits need not be numerically identical:

- sparse LD omits weak or distant off-diagonal entries;
- stored correlations and reconstructed cross-products have finite precision;
- BED and CSR implementations may maintain residual states differently;
- update scheduling and marker order can differ;
- route-specific prior or residual-adjustment settings can differ; and
- MCMC output contains Monte Carlo variation.

Agreement should therefore be assessed through posterior distributions,
marker-level patterns, predictions, variance summaries, and sensitivity
analyses rather than equality of individual MCMC draws.

## Validation and Diagnostics

Before fitting a summary-statistics model, verify the current code objects
against the corresponding mathematical quantities:

1. Every trait's `wy` vector has length $M$ and corresponds to $X^\top y_t$.
2. Every trait's `ww` vector has length $M$, contains finite positive values,
   and is compatible with the LD scaling.
3. `yy` has one marginal phenotype cross-product per trait for parallel
   single-trait fitting, or the joint MT route receives the required full
   trait cross-product information.
4. The supplied `n` corresponds to the sample used to calculate the associated
   summary statistics; trait-specific sample sizes and overlap assumptions are
   recorded where relevant.
5. Sparse-LD dimensions are $M\times M$, and marker order matches `wy` and
   `ww`.
6. `cls`, allele frequencies, `rows`, and `scale` choices are compatible
   between `bed_xtx_xty()` and sparse-LD construction.
7. Marker names, annotation rows, and posterior marker summaries use the same
   marker order and allele orientation.
8. Phenotypes are centered, or the intercept/centering convention is otherwise
   explicit.
9. The magnitude of `ww` is plausible for the genotype coding and sample size.
10. LD thresholds, windows, precision, reference sample, and construction
    provenance are recorded.

Useful implementation diagnostics include inspecting `stats$n`, `stats$m`,
`stats$scale`, `stats$min_xx`, `stats$mean_xx`, and `stats$max_xx`; reading CSR
metadata with `sparseLD_read_CSR()`; and comparing BED-direct and CSR fits when
the same individual-level data are available.

## Limitations

Summary-statistic inference cannot recover information that was never retained
or supplied.

- **Summary-statistic/LD compatibility:** `wy` and `ww` from one sample or
  genotype-scaling convention combined with LD from another imply an
  approximate and potentially biased likelihood.
- **LD-reference mismatch:** ancestry, allele frequencies, imputation quality,
  marker filtering, and sample selection can make reference LD differ from
  study LD.
- **Sparsification:** thresholding and windowing deliberately remove
  off-diagonal cross-product information.
- **Phenotype preprocessing:** unrecorded centering, scaling, covariate
  adjustment, or residualization changes the meaning of the code fields
  representing $X^\top y$ and $y^\top y$.
- **Multi-trait information:** marginal trait statistics do not identify
  cross-trait phenotype products or sample overlap.
- **Overlap assumptions:** incorrect pairwise overlap counts or phenotype
  covariance assumptions can distort full residual covariance inference.
- **Posterior summaries:** set contributions calculated from posterior means
  do not automatically propagate full posterior uncertainty.

These are model-input assumptions and approximation choices, not merely
implementation details.
